PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Dentist&rsquo;s Office — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the whole tooth check-up, step by step, so the chair feels like a game before the real visit.

What is this?

A dentist&rsquo;s office is where teeth get their check-ups: counted, cleaned, and protected from sugar bugs.

What does it mean?

Small habits, big teeth: the dentist is the coach who helps your smile win every day.

What does the child need to know?

You need brave sitting, an open mouth on request, and a toothbrush working at home twice a day — the dentist sees everything, you know.

Why this matters

Teeth are the only bones we show the world — and the only ones that can get holes. The dentist finds tiny trouble while it is still tiny.

What it teaches

Opening wide on request, sitting in a chair that leans, naming teeth (front, pointy, big grinders), and the twice-a-day brushing habit.

Words to learn

dentistteethtoothcheck-upmirrorpolishsugar bugsstickeropen wide

Say this to your child

“"Hop in the chair, open wide — AHH! The dentist counts: one, two, three... all here! No sugar bugs today! Now the polish — bzzzz — tickle, tickle — all shiny! Sticker, please!"”

Step by step

  1. Climb into the big chair — it leans back like a rocket ready for launch.
  2. Open wide and say ahh — the little mirror hops in for a look around.
  3. Count the teeth out loud: how many live in there today?
  4. Hunt for sugar bugs — spot them before they build a house.
  5. Polish! The spinning brush tickles, the teeth shine, and the treasure box pays out the sticker.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a giant tooth hangs over the striped awning of the dentist&rsquo;s office — nobody ever has to guess who works in this building.

Ask your child

"What do we say to open wide?" (ahh!) "Who counts our teeth?" (the dentist) "How do we keep sugar bugs away at home?" (brush, brush, brush — twice a day)

What your child can say or do

Your child might count the family&rsquo;s teeth at dinner (up to 32 per grown-up, they will learn), play dentist with a spoon mirror and a very firm "open wider, please", or demand the polish sound "bzzz" during bedtime brushing.

Out in the real world

American families visit the dentist&rsquo;s office; British families visit the dentist&rsquo;s surgery — same chair, same mirror, same sticker. First visits are kept short and friendly on purpose: sit, count, polish, treasure box, done.

Try it together

Doll dentist: count all the doll&rsquo;s teeth out loud, check with a spoon for a mirror, brush every single one with a real toothbrush, and pay for the visit with one pretend coin. The counting IS the practice.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we say for the dentist?" (open wide — ahh!) "How do we beat the sugar bugs?" (brushing twice a day, and the dentist&rsquo;s polish)

This lesson pairs with the Dentist&rsquo;s Office flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.
